title: Ages & Partnership
relevance: Campus OAs and aptitude rounds test ages via time-shifted ratios and partnership via Capital×Time profit splits, often wrapped as equity vesting or shared-resource billing.
company_notes: OA wrappers often frame partnership as startup equity vesting or AWS-style shared-resource billing; the Capital×Time math is unchanged.

phases.goal: Establish the present-age variable rule and the Capital×Time profit-share principle.

must_hit.point: Always set the present age as the variable; translate “N years ago” to x−N and “N years hence/later” to x+N, then form equations from the given ratio conditions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate picks present ages as unknowns and systematically offsets by N before writing any past/future ratio equation.

must_hit.point: Partnership profits are split in the ratio Capital×Time: if A invests C_A for T_A and B invests C_B for T_B, the profit ratio is C_A T_A : C_B T_B.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states profit shares track investment weight = capital times duration, not capital alone when times differ.

probes: How do you choose variables and rewrite “N years ago / hence” in an ages ratio problem?
When two partners invest unequal amounts for unequal times, how is profit shared?

hints.1: Start from present ages, not a past snapshot.
hints.2: Ages: present = x, past = x−N, future = x+N. Partnership: weight each partner by capital times months invested.
hints.3: Write present ages as variables, offset by N for the stated time, equate ratios; for partnership use C_A T_A : C_B T_B.

phases.goal: Show exact setups for age equations, constant age-gap, equal-time capital ratios, and multi-phase capital weights.

must_hit.point: From a present age ratio (e.g. mother:daughter = 7:1 as 7x and x), apply the past ratio only after subtracting the elapsed years from both ages, then solve the resulting equation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes (7x−4)/(x−4)=19 (or analogous), clears, and recovers present ages before answering a future-age ask.

must_hit.point: The age difference between two people is constant at any time, so a past “A was k times B” condition can be solved using that fixed difference on past ages.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate notes the gap is unchanged (e.g. still 24 ten years ago), sets past ages as ky and y with ky−y equal to the gap, then adds years back to present.

must_hit.point: If everyone invests for the same duration, profit splits by capital ratio alone; if someone joins mid-year or capital changes mid-year, compute each phase’s Capital×Time and sum weights before sharing profit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate uses capital-only parts when times match, otherwise builds weights like (C1×t1)+(C2×t2) or months-after-join, then multiplies profit by that partner’s share of total parts.

must_hit.point: For a present-age sum with a past ratio, the sum of ages N years ago equals the present sum minus 2N (two people), then apply the past ratio parts to that past sum.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate subtracts 2N from the present sum, splits the past sum by the past ratio (e.g. 3:1 → 3/4 of past sum), then adds N to get present age.

probes: Walk through setting up a present ratio plus a different past ratio as equations.
Partner Y joins after several months of a year—how do you compute Y’s profit weight?
How can a fixed age gap replace a present-age variable when the multiple is given for the past?

hints.1: Offset every age to the same clock time before writing a ratio or product.
hints.2: Ages: present ratio → variables; past ratio → subtract years first. Partnership: months invested = year length minus join delay; changing capital → sum of phase weights.
hints.3: Example shapes: (7x−4)/(x−4)=19; past gap 5y−y=24; same-time capital 3:4; mid-year join uses 8 months of 12; changing capital (4000×8)+(6000×4).

phases.goal: Contrast capital-only vs Capital×Time splits and salary-off-the-top vs pure capital division.

must_hit.point: Equal investment duration → profit by capital ratio only; unequal durations (late join, early exit, or mid-year capital change) → must use Capital×Time weights instead of raw capital.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains when dropping time is valid and when omitting months would mis-share profit.

must_hit.point: A working partner may take a stated percent of total profit as salary first; only the remainder is divided by capital ratio, so total receipt = salary + capital share of the remainder.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate separates 20% off the top, splits 80% by 2:3 capital parts, and combines salary plus remainder share to recover total profit from a given receipt.

probes: When is splitting by capital alone enough, and when must you multiply by time?
How does a working-partner salary change the profit equations versus a pure capital partnership?

hints.1: Ask whether every rupee was deployed for the same number of months.
hints.2: Same months → capital ratio; different months or changing capital → sum Capital×Time. Salary cases: peel percent first, then split what’s left.
hints.3: Same-year full investment → e.g. 45000:60000 = 3:4 of profit; late join or capital change → weighted months; 20% salary then 2:3 of the remaining 80%.

phases.goal: Map OA story wrappers (founder equity, shared cloud billing) back to Capital×Time partnership math.

must_hit.point: Startup founder dividends based on capital-time contribution are ordinary partnership weights: months active after join (and explicit stay length on exit) times capital, then profit parts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate converts join delays and early exits into months invested, forms Capital×Time ratios, and allocates the founders’ dividend by those parts.

must_hit.point: Shared cloud/cluster bills split by node-usage time use the same idea: treat nodes as “capital” and hours as “time,” then charge by that weight ratio.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate computes each project’s nodes×hours, forms the ratio of weights, and multiplies the monthly bill by that project’s share of total parts.

probes: Three founders join and leave at different months—how do you compute one founder’s dividend share?
How would you allocate a monthly cluster bill across projects with different node counts and daily hours?

hints.1: Ignore the SaaS/cloud story labels; recover capital and duration.
hints.2: Weight = money×months active, or nodes×hours; then share = weight/total × payout.
hints.3: Late join → fewer months; early exit → only stated stay months; billing → nodes×hours parts of the monthly cost.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: If all partners invest for the same duration, profit follows the capital ratio alone. If join times, exit times, or capital amounts change mid-period, each partner’s share must use Capital×Time (summing phase weights when capital changes), not raw capital.

tradeoffs.topic: Working-partner salary then capital split vs pure capital split
tradeoffs.strong_answer: With a working-partner salary, a stated percent of total profit is taken off the top first; only the remainder is divided by capital ratio. Pure capital partnership applies the capital (or Capital×Time) ratio to the entire profit with no salary peel.

gotchas.trap: Applying a sum, product, or difference constraint to a ratio from a different point in time without shifting ages.
gotchas.correction: If the ratio describes the situation N years ago, offset all present ages by −N (or use past ages explicitly) before imposing that ratio; never mix a present sum/product with an unshifted past ratio.

gotchas.trap: Treating a mid-year join as a full year of investment.
gotchas.correction: Months invested equal the period actually funded—e.g. joining after 4 months of a 12-month year means 8 months in the Capital×Time weight.

gotchas.trap: Assuming an early-leaving partner stays through year-end.
gotchas.correction: Use only the stated active duration (e.g. stays 4 months) in Capital×Time, not “from join until month 12.”
